analysis:
The PR changes only documentation: docs/architecture/inference.md (head lines 1030-1047 per the range map) and docs/developer/test.md (head lines 322-345). I examined the supplied head excerpts of inference.md (lines 1640-2266) and the full patches. The changed text itself adds no executable code, no wire or protocol change, and no attestation, authorization or encryption change.

The new documentation describes a PromptTokenCache. It reuses token IDs of previously seen prompt pieces within the same prefix-cache scope. It states that reuse never crosses a cache scope, that sampled background comparisons disable reuse on a mismatch, and that DARKBLOOM_TTFT_PROMPT_CACHE=0 restores the unchanged path. This is relevant to T-041 (cross-tenant prefix-cache sharing and TTFT timing oracle) and A-001, and I checked it against the T-041 cache scope model. Nothing in the description widens at-rest exposure. The cache is in-memory and scoped per cacheSalt. Scope separation is documented, but the implementation (PromptTokenCache.swift) is not supplied, so I cannot confirm it. If the implementation keys on anything other than the coordinator-authored cacheSalt, or persists pieces, it could add a timing oracle (faster tokenization on a hit) and a possible cross-account side channel. The threat model's T-041 text may need to mention this in-memory tokenization-reuse path. The documented scope binding is a design claim, not verified behavior. The documented 4-core parallel encoding and the loop-rewritten Gemma/GPT-OSS templates are also not verifiable here. A rewrite that diverges from the original render could change prompt tokens. The documented background comparison is intended to catch this.

The test doc adds a test command and a benchmark flag, with no security-relevant surface. I identified no concrete security regression. The remaining question for the code PR is whether the implementation actually enforces scope-keyed reuse and the fail-closed mismatch behavior.
